title: Composition on V_n as ideal multiplication in ℤ[2√f]: certificates as a 'box' in a narrow class group
connection: COMPOSITION_ES: V_n values at μ are the fibre over a fixed order-2 narrow class δ of the box of primitive ideals of norm dividing μ. ES ⇔ the box meets δ with an extra condition (B = 1).
why: Class-group 'boxes' (ideals of bounded norm generating/hitting a class) are a native class-field-theory question, with results via Bach's bound under GRH and unconditional Lamzouri-type results.
first_step: Calibrate: for μ in a window, size of box vs narrow class number; check whether GRH-Bach bounds would put the box onto δ (they handle generation, not hitting one class with norm constraints).

title: Heegner points / CM points equidistribution (Duke) for the lattice meeting point
connection: LATTICE_MEETING moves the slice inside Cl(−4p); Duke's theorem says CM points of discriminant −4p equidistribute on the modular curve. Certificates are CM points landing in a thin region (near the cusp, Y small).
why: Duke's theorem with explicit rates (Iwaniec's bound for half-integral-weight coefficients) is a pointwise-in-p existence statement for regions of size ≫ p^{−δ}. ES needs regions of size ≈ p^{−1/2}·polylog.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the 'certificate region' for CM points of disc −4p and compare with the best-known equidistribution error p^{−1/28}-type.
refs: Duke, Hyperbolic distribution problems and half-integral weight Maass forms (Invent. 1988)

title: Genus theory and the 2-part of Cl(−4p): ES sign as a genus character value
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), Cl(−4p) has 2-rank 1, and genus characters are (·/p) and χ_{−4}. Certificate ideals of norm e must lie in a principal genus or its complement; the slot lemma's mod-4 condition may be the 4-rank (Rédei) symbol.
why: Rédei symbols and 4-ranks are explicit and computable. If the ES sign is a Rédei symbol of the certificate ideal, the structure is governed by governing fields (Stevenhagen, Smith).
first_step: For p < 10⁵, compute the Rédei-matrix data of Q(√−p), Q(√−2p) and compare with p's ES₅ certificate statistics (sign distributions by level).
refs: Stevenhagen, Rédei reciprocity, governing fields and negative Pell (2018; check)

title: Quaternion order Λ_{d,m}: reduced-norm representation of p by a ternary sublattice
connection: QUATERNION_ES Lemma 1.2: Λ_{d,m} = ℤ⟨u,v⟩ with u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1 is an order. Type I data are elements of prescribed norm/trace. ES becomes 'p is represented by a specific ternary norm form attached to (d,m)'.
why: Representation by ternary forms attached to orders has a theory: Gross lattices, Eichler orders, spinor genera. A family over (d,m) gives many forms, any of which suffices.
first_step: For each (d,m) ≤ 20 compute the Gross lattice (trace-zero part) and its genus; check whether p's representability by that genus is automatic (local conditions only) and whether spinor exceptions arise.

title: F₂-linear algebra: ES₅ failure ⇔ a linear system over F₂ in the Legendre symbols of small primes
connection: (A/p) = ∏ (q/p)^{v_q(A)}. ES₅ failure ⇔ all A ∈ S₃(p) have Σ v_q(A)·ε_q ≡ 0 (mod 2), where ε_q = [(q/p) = −1]. This is a linear system over F₂ in the unknown vector ε (the 'quadratic character of p on primes').
why: The exact linear-algebra form shows that failure is consistent iff the exponent-vector matrix of S₃(p) has the actual ε in its right kernel. Rank considerations give a sharp combinatorial necessary condition.
first_step: For p < 10⁶ compute rank_F₂ of the exponent matrix of S₃(p) (over primes dividing elements) and the codimension of the failure space; record the minimum over p.

title: Borwein–Choi's xy+yz+zx theorem as the closest proved sibling of I3/U(n)
connection: Borwein–Choi: there are at most 19 integers not of the form xy+yz+zx (x,y,z ≥ 1). Eighteen are known, and the 19th is excluded under GRH. The form is classified via class groups of Q(√−n), using (x+z)(y+z) = n + z². I3 is n = tuv−u−v ⇔ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1.
why: It is structurally parallel (a factorisation of n + (shift) with constraints) and is proved up to one possible exception via idoneal-type class-number arguments. The I3/U analogue would be 'finitely many failures, all but one effective'.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and translate: for which discriminants does 'tn+1 has no factorisation (tu−1)(tv−1)' force a class-group condition (exponent ≤ 2) on Q(√−?)?
refs: Borwein–Choi, On the representations of xy+yz+zx, Exp. Math. 9 (2000) 153–158

title: Class-number-one-type ineffectivity: is I3's exceptional list finite by a Siegel-type argument?
connection: Chowla proved finiteness of idoneal numbers via Siegel's (ineffective) class-number bound. If I3 failure at n forced a large class group to have a small exponent (an 'idoneal-type' condition), Siegel–Tatuzawa would give finiteness of exceptions up to one.
why: It is the only known mechanism turning a 'polylog-witness' representation problem into a pointwise theorem (with ineffectivity). It is the (R)-rigidity type of FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Look for a map: I3 failure at n ⇒ the class group of some order of disc −D(n) has exponent ≤ 2 (or bounded); test on the known I3 exceptions.
refs: Chowla, An extension of Heilbronn's class-number theorem (1934)

title: Artin-type: elements of L₃(p) with maximal 2-part of order; links to Artin's conjecture methods
connection: ES₅ ⇔ some A ∈ L₃(p) has v₂(ord_p A) = v₂(p − 1). Artin-type problems (Heath-Brown, Gupta–Murty) prove that one of a few fixed integers is a primitive root mod infinitely many p. Here the candidate set depends on p.
why: It translates ES₅ into the language of multiplicative orders, where Chebotarev in Kummer extensions Q(ζ_{2^k}, A^{1/2^k}) is the native tool, but A depends on p (B2).
first_step: Check whether a fixed-A family (e.g. A = 2·3 − 1 = 5 from the word (2,3,v)) with v₂(ord_p 5) = v₂(p−1) covers a Chebotarev set of primes, and compute its density.
refs: Heath-Brown, Artin's conjecture for primitive roots (1986)

title: Hurwitz quaternions and metacommutation: ES certificates as factorisation patterns
connection: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternion factorisations of a norm-N element are unique up to metacommutation (Conway–Smith; Cohn–Kumar studied the metacommutation permutation). Certificates involve factorisations of p-tied norms in quaternion orders (QUATERNION_ES).
why: Metacommutation is a canonical permutation on factorisations with computable sign/cycle structure. The ES sign might be a metacommutation invariant.
first_step: For small p, compute the factorisations relevant to QUATERNION_ES Type I data in the Hurwitz order and the metacommutation permutation's sign.
refs: Cohn–Kumar, Metacommutation of Hurwitz primes (Proc. AMS 2015)

title: Gaussian periods / cyclotomic: (A/p) via the quadratic Gauss sum and certificates as cyclotomic units
connection: (A/p) = σ_A(√p*)/√p* in Q(ζ_p). Words give A with AA* = tp + 1, i.e. A·A* ≡ 1 (mod p), so σ_A σ_{A*} = id. The ES sign is the action of σ_A on the quadratic subfield.
why: Galois-theoretic language: ES₅ ⇔ some word's Galois element σ_A ∈ Gal(Q(ζ_p)/Q) is non-trivial on Q(√p). This connects to Galois-module structure of cyclotomic units (Sinnott) if words relate to units.
first_step: Look for a cyclotomic unit or Gauss-sum expression naturally indexed by words (e.g. (1 − ζ^A)/(1 − ζ)) whose norm to Q(√p) is sign-sensitive.

title: Real quadratic order of γ_w: words as reduced cycles and the sign as a genus/narrow-class invariant
connection: γ_w ∈ SL₂(ℤ) hyperbolic determines a real quadratic order of discriminant (tr γ_w)² − 4 and an ideal class (Latimer–MacDuffee). The ES sign might be a genus character of that class evaluated at p.
why: Latimer–MacDuffee is an exact bijection between conjugacy classes of matrices and ideal classes. The sign then becomes a class-group statement in a family of real quadratic fields.
first_step: Compute the ideal class for γ_w (p < 300) and evaluate genus characters; check whether one equals (A/p).

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli: Type I as p | N(j(τ₁) − j(τ₂))
connection: Gross–Zagier: p divides N(j(τ₁) − j(τ₂)) iff the two CM orders embed simultaneously into a maximal order of B_{p,∞} (with an explicit formula). QUATERNION_ES shows Type I(p) ⇔ an 'x = 2 collision' of CM orders in B_{p,∞}.
why: It may give a closed criterion: ES Type I at p ⇔ p divides a specific singular-moduli difference. The Gross–Zagier formula expresses the exponent as a sum over representations of binary forms.
first_step: Check numerically for p < 500 whether Type I certificate existence at level d matches p | N(j(√−d)·…) for the orders appearing in Λ_{d,m}.

title: Ibukiyama's explicit maximal orders O(q,r) in B_{p,∞} vs the ES orders Λ_{d,m}
connection: Ibukiyama gives explicit maximal orders of B_{p,∞} in terms of q ≡ 3 mod 8 with (−q/p) = −1 and r² ≡ −p mod q. ES's Λ_{d,m} are orders in definite algebras defined by u² = −d, v² = −m, uv + vu = 1. Embedding Λ_{d,m} into O(q,r) links certificates to the choice of auxiliary prime q.
why: Ibukiyama orders are the standard computational model. The auxiliary-prime choice resembles ES's least-QNR dependence (q with (−q/p) = −1).
first_step: For p < 200, test which Λ_{d,m} embed into Ibukiyama orders with small q and compare with certificate levels.
refs: Ibukiyama, On maximal orders of division quaternion algebras over the rational number field with certain optimal embeddings (Nagoya 1982)

title: Egyptian fractions over the p-adics with archimedean positivity: a 'local-global' table per place
connection: For each place v, ES is solvable over ℤ_v (and positively over ℝ). The obstruction is global. An adelic-orbit/Tamagawa view gives the BM main term as ∏_v vol(U_n(ℤ_v)). The 2-adic factor carries the slot-lemma condition.
why: It records the native adelic computation that the repo already uses (BM_CORRECTED_COUNT); here the point is a per-place table of the slot-lemma 2-adic measure.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic measure of the set of words with some pentagon entry ≡ 0 (mod 4), as a function of p mod 8.

title: Small levels as norm forms: level-t failure for t ∈ {3,4,6,8,12} ⇔ tp+1 is (roughly) a norm from Q(√−t)-type orders
connection: A divisor of tp + 1 that is ≡ −1 (mod t) exists iff some prime factor lies outside the subgroup generated by the classes splitting appropriately. For t = 4 this means 'some prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4)', so level-4 failure ⇔ 4p+1 has only prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) ⇔ 4p+1 is a sum of two coprime squares. Similar statements hold for t = 3 (norms from ℤ[ω]).
why: This makes the first levels' failure a Landau–Ramanujan-type 'values of a linear form that are norms' property. Writing 4p+1 = (2a+1)² + (2b)² gives p = a² + a + b², a quadratic polynomial in two variables. Iwaniec (1972) proved that suitable quadratic polynomials in two variables represent infinitely many primes; if his theorem applies here with the primitivity condition gcd(2a+1, 2b) = 1, it gives a PROVED infinite family of primes failing level 4 (check).
first_step: Compute the density of p for which all levels t ∈ {3,4,6,8,12} fail (simultaneous norm conditions), and the sieve-dimension of that set; compare with data.
refs: Iwaniec, Primes of the type φ(x,y) + A where φ is a quadratic form (Acta Arith. 1972)

title: Positive definite binary forms of discriminant −4(tp+1)… and the A/A* pairing as an ambiguous-form question
connection: Factorisations N = A·A* correspond to ambiguous forms/ideals of discriminant related to N. Words are factorisations with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t). Genus theory of disc −4N tells which ambiguous classes exist.
why: Gauss's genus theory counts factorisations as ambiguous classes, and the mod-t condition becomes a genus-character condition, a native class-group statement.
first_step: For small t, compute the genus characters of the ambiguous forms of disc −4N_t and identify which genus the word factorisations occupy.

title: Sum-of-two-squares parametrisation p = a² + b² as an ES parameter space (Gaussian Type II)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4) write p = a² + b². ES certificates might be organised by Gaussian integers: e.g. 4Cp + 1 = 4C(a² + b²) + 1 factors in ℤ[i]-related ways, and the divisor class −1 (mod 4C) might be read off a Gaussian factorisation.
why: It is a natural extra structure that exactly the hard primes possess (p ≡ 1 mod 4). If certificates correlate with (a, b), the Gaussian angle gives a new handle (Hecke equidistribution).
first_step: For p < 10⁶, compute (a mod 8, b mod 8, a mod 3, …) and the least certificate level; search for a deterministic rule using (a,b).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Universal-form reduction: a map from representations by a universal quadratic form to ES certificates
connection: Linnik/Watson reduced 7 cubes to ternary forms; Hilbert used identities + Lagrange. Seek a quadratic form Q_p (or a fixed universal Q) and an explicit rational map Φ such that every representation Q(v) = g(p) yields an ES solution for p; universality/three-squares then proves ES.
why: Not a polynomial identity in p (so Mordell–Schinzel does not apply directly); the map may depend on the representation. Must be compatible with T1 (Type I/II fail at odd squares).
first_step: Search small Φ: take ES (★) triples (u,B,C) for many p and test whether u, B, C, or 4uC−1 are systematically sums of two/three squares with coordinates linked to p.

title: Ternary-form reduction with Duke–Schulze-Pillot as the closing theorem
connection: Linnik's 7 cubes: identity reduces the problem to n − (cubes) being represented by a ternary quadratic form in an AP, closed by ternary-form theory. ES: find an ES-certificate family equivalent to 'some N(p) is primitively represented by a positive ternary form in a fixed genus'.
why: DSP gives every sufficiently large n in the spinor genus (ineffectively) — an 'all large p' ES theorem even if ineffective would be new.
first_step: Search the (★)/b=1/ES₅ certificate shapes for a sum-of-three-squares interpretation (e.g. 4Cp+1 = d d' with d = x²+y²+z²-type constraint); test on data.
refs: Watson, J. London Math. Soc. 26 (1951) 153-156 (A simple proof that all large integers are sums of at most seven cubes)

title: Dedekind's Gaussian-integer proof analogue: an order where ES(p) ⟺ p is a norm
connection: Fermat two squares follows from ℤ[i] being Euclidean. Find a (possibly noncommutative) ring/order R and norm-like map such that ES certificates ↔ elements of 'norm' p with congruence side conditions; then a class-number-one/Euclidean property gives existence.
why: Quaternion orders and theta quotients already appear in the repo; the missing piece is a ring whose class number is 1 and whose norm condition matches the ES congruences.
first_step: Read the quaternion-order memos (git grep -il quaternion); compute class/type numbers of the orders arising there.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Class number one in the genus: search for an ES-encoding lattice with a one-class genus
connection: Gauss's three squares: local solvability + one class in the genus of x²+y²+z² ⇒ global. ES is locally solvable everywhere (Bright–Loughran); if ES(p) ⟺ a lattice L represents an invariant of p, and gen(L) has one class (or one spinor genus), ES follows.
why: The most classical local→global mechanism; repo has quaternion/lattice reformulations whose class numbers may never have been computed.
first_step: For each lattice reformulation in the repo, compute the class number of its genus (Sage/Magma genus enumeration) for small parameters.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Correlate f_I(p), R(p) with class numbers h(−4p), h(−kp)
connection: Duke/Iwaniec: representation numbers of ternary forms ≈ class numbers. If some ES count correlates with h(−kp) for small k, a class-number-sized main term may be hidden in a weighted ES count.
why: Cheap test of whether ES counts carry class-number information beyond the BM/genus layer.
first_step: For primes p ≤ 10⁷, regress R(p)/log²p and f_I(p)/log²p on h(−4p)/√p, h(p)·reg/√p and L(1,(·/p)); report partial correlations.

title: Heath-Brown's 'one of three' for ES windows
connection: Heath-Brown: among three multiplicatively independent integers satisfying non-square conditions (e.g. three distinct primes), one is a primitive root for infinitely many p. ES windows: failure at window e requires the divisor classes of N_e = (p+e)/4 to avoid −1 in their ratio set (often: lie in an index-2 subgroup without −1). Show three suitably independent windows cannot all fail.
why: Pigeonhole over several candidate families is an every-type argument that needs no single family to work.
first_step: For (★)-failing primes, record for small windows e the subgroup generated by the prime factors of N_e mod e; look for algebraic relations among three windows that make simultaneous avoidance impossible.
refs: Heath-Brown, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986) 27-38 (Artin's conjecture for primitive roots)

title: Inverse Frey: encode the failure of ES at p as an object with impossible properties
connection: Frey/Ribet/Wiles: a hypothetical solution yields an elliptic curve whose mod-ℓ representation would come from a nonexistent level-2 form. ES failure gives no point, but it gives a huge family of constraints (no divisor of 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod 4C, for all C). Package these constraints as a Galois/automorphic object (e.g. a 'character' on level structures) and seek a rigidity contradiction.
why: The FLT pattern 'counterexample ⇒ object ⇒ contradiction' is the archetypal every-n proof; ES's failure data are rich enough to define objects.
first_step: Formalise the failure data as a function F_p(C, a) = 1[class a mod 4C contains a divisor of 4Cp+1]; check whether ES failure makes F_p multiplicative/character-like in C (it would be in the square-mimicking profinite model).

title: Annihilator theory in (ℤ/4C)*: Stickelberger-type relations among divisor classes
connection: Mihăilescu's proof uses annihilators of cyclotomic class groups. The classes of prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)* across many C are linked (the same p); look for annihilator-type relations that prevent all of them from avoiding −1.
why: Odd: ES failure is a statement about a family of subgroups indexed by C; group-ring relations between the families might be forced by the common p.
first_step: Compute for fixed p the vectors (class of q mod 4C) for primes q | 4Cp+1, C ≤ 200, and search for linear relations in the group ring that hold for all p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Cyclotomic size argument: 'non-certificate part' of Π_C(4Cp+1) must be small
connection: Bang–Zsigmondy: Φ_n(a) is large but its non-primitive part is tiny (only the largest prime of n), so a primitive prime exists. ES analogue: bound the part of Π_{C≤X}(4Cp+1) made of primes that cannot participate in any certificate, and show it is smaller than the whole.
why: A size argument needs no equidistribution; it uses only the explicit CRT census of prime factors (cf. Erdős–Bertrand item).
first_step: Define 'certificate-capable' primes q (those with 4c_q | (q+1)k-type relations) and compute log of the incapable part vs. Σ log(4Cp+1) for test p.

title: Dirichlet–Pell pigeonhole on near-certificates in M₂(ℤ)
connection: Pell is solvable for every non-square D by: infinitely many (x,y) with bounded norm defect, two with the same defect k and residues mod k, divide them to get norm 1. ES Type I/II fail exactly at odd squares — the Pell exception shape. In the SL₂ form, look for near-certificate matrices with bounded defect; two congruent ones give a quotient that is an exact certificate.
why: Pigeonhole + group law is the cleanest every-n mechanism whose only failures are squares; T1 must appear as the reason the quotient fails at squares.
first_step: Define defect for matrices [[a,p],[c,d]] (e.g. det = 1 + δ, or a ≡ −1 only mod c/δ); generate many for a given p and test whether quotients of pairs with equal defect yield exact certificates.

title: Non-vanishing criterion (Gross–Zagier style) for the existence of a certificate
connection: Gross–Zagier: a Heegner point is non-torsion iff L′(E,1) ≠ 0 — existence from an analytic non-vanishing. ES: seek a curve/abelian variety A_p with a canonical point whose non-triviality is equivalent to (or implies) an ES certificate, so that a non-vanishing statement proves ES.
why: Converts existence into non-vanishing of a special value, where analytic tools work for every member of a family.
first_step: Look for elliptic fibrations of the ES surface U_p (e.g. fix x/y = λ) and compute whether the integral points relate to multiples of a canonical point.

title: Mollified variance to identify which characters explain R's fluctuations
connection: Mollifiers (Selberg/Levinson/Conrey) dampen large values by a short Dirichlet polynomial. Fit R(n)/M(n) − 1 by a short combination of Legendre symbols (n/ℓ), ℓ ≤ L; the residual variance after mollification measures what remains beyond the genus/BM layer.
why: Tells whether ES fluctuations are dominated by a few small characters (then a Heilbronn-type split is promising) or are spread out (then they are 'X(p)' noise).
first_step: Least-squares fit on n ≤ 10⁷ in Mordell-hard classes; report explained variance as a function of L.

title: Potential ES: count solutions over a quadratic field and use Galois parity
connection: Potential automorphy proves things over extensions and descends via Brauer induction. ES over O_K for real quadratic K: Gal(K/ℚ) acts on K-solutions of 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z with totally positive x,y,z; fixed points are ℚ-solutions. If the number of K-solutions in a Galois-stable finite window is odd, a rational solution exists.
why: Parity across a Galois action is a descent mechanism that needs no analysis over ℚ.
first_step: For K = ℚ(√2), ℚ(√5) and small p, enumerate totally positive integral solutions with norms bounded (finite after fixing a fundamental domain for units) and compute the parity of the count of non-rational ones.
refs: Barnet-Lamb-Geraghty-Harris-Taylor, Publ. RIMS 47 (2011) 29-98 (A family of Calabi-Yau varieties and potential automorphy II)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Values of rational quadratic forms with congruence: does ES's (degenerate) quadric relate to the exceptional rational case of EMM?
connection: Eskin–Margulis–Mozes: for irrational forms counts are asymptotic, while rational forms of signature (2,1)/(2,2) have exceptional logarithmic behaviour. ES's quadric ad − pc is rational but degenerate (rank-2 quadratic part, linear in c), so EMM does not apply directly; ask whether a nondegenerate model (e.g. after eliminating c via a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c) falls in the EMM exceptional regime and whether the log-excess there mirrors the log²p main term.
why: A dictionary between ES's polylog main term and the known exceptional counts of rational quadrics could import their methods.
first_step: Read EMM's treatment of rational forms (Annals 1998) and compute the predicted count for ad − pc ∈ {1} with |a|,|d| ≤ T, c ≤ T.

title: Representations with linear side conditions: ES certificates as constrained quaternion norms
connection: Machiavelo–Tsopanidis proved Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture (four squares with a linear condition) for every n. If ES certificates can be phrased as 'p (or 4Cp+1) is a norm from an order with a linear side condition on coordinates', their arithmetic arguments may transfer.
why: Linear side conditions on norm representations are exactly the shape of ES congruence constraints.
first_step: Read Machiavelo–Tsopanidis' method; try to phrase (★) as N(α) = 4Cp+1 with α in an order and a linear congruence on α's coordinates.
refs: arXiv:2003.02592 (Machiavelo-Tsopanidis, Zhi-Wei Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture and variations)

title: Type I via binary forms: divisors of p² + 4c²d in classes mod 4cd
connection: Class field theory decides which primes are represented by which forms. Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd). Divisors of values of X² + 4dY² are constrained by genus/class-group characters of disc −16d; the condition f ≡ −p couples them to p. Compute exactly which classes mod 4cd are possible for divisors, and show −p is excluded exactly when p is a square (T1).
why: Puts Type I in CFT language where every-p statements (Chebotarev, ring class fields) are standard.
first_step: For small d, c enumerate possible classes of divisors of p² + 4c²d mod 4cd via genus characters, and compare with −p's class; verify the T1 exclusion at squares.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x^2 + ny^2 (1989)

title: p-adic interpolation along exponential families (Skolem–Mahler–Lech)
connection: SML proves zero sets of linear recurrences are periodic + finite via p-adic analytic interpolation. ES along n_s = a·b^s + c: certificate conditions involve divisors of 4C·n_s + 1 = 4Ca·b^s + (4Cc + 1), an exponential sequence; p-adic interpolation of 'divisibility by a fixed d' gives periodic structure in s, possibly proving ES for open families like 15·2^s + 1 by periodic covering + finitely many checks.
why: The repo already proved several exponential families via windows; SML-type periodicity could organise the remaining ones.
first_step: For 15·2^s + 1 compute, for each small (C, d) with d ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the set of s with d | 4C·n_s + 1 (periodic in s); check whether a finite union of these covers all s.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0304] Implement for 15·2^s + 1 and 4^s + 297 with d ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 10³.

title: Mordell's class-number formula for yz + zx + xy = p as an exact power-size count
connection: Duke/Iwaniec exploit class-number-sized representation counts. Mordell (1923) gives, for prime n, the number of positive solutions of yz + zx + xy = n as 3G(n) − 3 (G class-number type). ES solutions satisfy σ₂(x,y,z) = 4σ₃/p; scaling Type II solutions (y = pY, z = pZ) gives p·YZ = x(4YZ − Y − Z), a σ₂-type relation. Look for a bijection or injection from a subset of Mordell's solutions (power-many) to ES certificates.
why: Would tie ES to an exact class-number count (power-size, every p), the Duke template.
first_step: For small primes, list Mordell's solutions of yz + zx + xy = p (or = 4p, kp) and test which ones transform into ES solutions via simple rational maps.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0182] Take Mordell's prime-n formula; then for ES solutions of small p tabulate m = xy+yz+zx and the class-number formula's prediction at n = m.

title: Modular units / Weber functions as certificate generators
connection: Heegner and Stark solved class number one through values of modular functions at CM points giving explicit Diophantine equations. Look for modular functions whose values at CM points related to p (disc −4p, −16p) are algebraic integers that factor into ES certificate data.
why: CM values give 'always-existing' algebraic objects attached to p; if their norms produce divisors in the right classes, existence follows.
first_step: Compute norms of Weber-function values f(√−p) or of singular moduli j((1+√−p)/2) differences for small p and check their prime factors against −1 (mod 4C) classes for the relevant C.

title: Pell-shaped conjecture: Type I ∪ II for all odd non-squares beyond a finite list
connection: Pell is solvable exactly for non-squares. ES Type I/II fail at all odd squares (T1) and, per the repo, U(n) fails at odd squares plus {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}. Formulate the precise 'Pell-shaped' conjecture (Type I ∪ II solvable for every odd non-square n outside an explicit finite list) and treat it as the natural target with the right exception set.
why: A conjecture whose exception set is exactly squares + finite list has the shape of classical every-n theorems (Pell, three squares).
first_step: Extend the Type I ∪ II census over odd non-squares (not just primes) to 10⁹ and confirm the exception list.

title: Quaternion (Hurwitz) proof of four squares: Euclidean order as the 'every p' engine
connection: Lagrange's theorem has a proof via the Hurwitz order being (left) Euclidean: p = ππ̄ factors, giving p as a norm. ES quaternion reformulations (repo) would need an order with a Euclidean-like property relative to a congruence structure tied to 4C.
why: If the relevant order (or its Eichler sub-order of level 4C) has class number one for small C, ES at those levels follows from factorisation.
first_step: Compute class numbers of Eichler orders of level 4C in the Hurwitz quaternion algebra (Sage) for C ≤ 20 and compare with which levels never fail.

title: Genus-theory exclusion at squares mirrors the 4^a(8b+7) exclusion
connection: Three squares fail exactly on 4^a(8b+7) — a local obstruction at 2. T1 is a global (reciprocity) exclusion at odd squares for Type I/II. Look for a ternary/quaternary encoding where the T1 exclusion becomes a local obstruction (at 2 or at an auxiliary prime) after a change of variables, which would make it 'genus visible'.
why: If T1 could be made local in some encoding, the remaining problem would be a pure genus-to-class question.
first_step: Test encodings: n ↦ 4Cn + 1 for small C; at odd squares n = m², check whether 4Cm² + 1's divisor-class failure is explained by local conditions at 2 or at primes dividing C.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Corrected local-global: formulate ES sub-routes with their reciprocity exceptions removed
connection: After the Apollonian disproof, the corrected conjecture excludes the reciprocity families. For ES sub-routes, formulate 'corrected' versions (e.g. Type I/II for all non-squares; (★) for all p outside an explicit reciprocity-defined set) and test which corrected statements have finite exception sets.
why: Ensures the targets are the right ones before attempting proofs.
first_step: Use the repo's census data to fit, for each sub-route, its failure set to explicit reciprocity conditions; report residual sporadic failures.
refs: arXiv:2307.02749 (Haag-Kertzer-Rickards-Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false)

title: Kummer-style 'regular' primes for ES: an invariant κ(p) that makes ES provable
connection: Kummer proved FLT for regular primes (p ∤ class number) long before Wiles. Look for an arithmetic invariant κ(p) (class number of ℚ(√−p), 2-rank/4-rank, parity of the fundamental unit norm of ℚ(√p), ℓ(p)) such that ES (or a sub-route) is provable for all p with κ(p) in some set, giving an infinite every-p family.
why: Partial every-p theorems on natural infinite sets of Mordell-hard primes do not yet exist; Kummer's theorem is the historical model.
first_step: Correlate (★)/ES₅ counts with κ(p) candidates for p ≤ 10⁸ and look for an invariant whose small/large values guarantee many certificates.

title: Limiting distribution of R(p)/M_BM(p) (a Sato–Tate/Cohen–Lenstra-type law)
connection: Sato–Tate identified the exact limiting law of normalised a_p. For ES, determine the limiting distribution of R(p)/M_BM(p) (and of f(p)/log³p) as p → ∞ through Mordell-hard primes; its behaviour near 0 is what decides ES heuristically.
why: A precise conjectural law with a computable left tail sharpens the heuristic case for ES and indicates which normalisation is 'right'.
first_step: Histogram R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes in windows at 10⁶, 10⁸, 10¹⁰; test convergence and fit the left tail.
refs: Barnet-Lamb-Geraghty-Harris-Taylor, Publ. RIMS 47 (2011) 29-98 (A family of Calabi-Yau varieties and potential automorphy II)

title: Class-number parity (genus theory, Rédei) as the source of oddness for a Zagier-type argument
connection: Heath-Brown's/Zagier's proofs use a set whose size parity is forced. Natural sets attached to p have sizes tied to class numbers h(−4p), h(−8p), whose parities/2-parts are governed by genus theory and Rédei symbols. Find an ES-related finite set whose cardinality equals (up to known even terms) such a class number with known parity.
why: Supplies the 'odd cardinality' input a parity proof needs from established theory.
first_step: Compute |S_p| for candidate sets (e.g. reduced forms of disc −16p with an extra congruence) and compare parity with h(−4p), h(−8p) and Rédei-symbol predictions.

title: Genus-theoretic parametrisations: Mordell-hard primes as values of principal-genus forms
connection: Gauss's genus theory: p is a square mod 840-type moduli iff p lies in principal genera of the relevant discriminants, so p = Q(x, y) for a form Q in a principal genus (disc −4·210 etc.). Seek certificate families polynomial in (x, y) for p = Q(x, y), exploiting that Mordell-hard classes are exactly where these representations exist.
why: Turns 'square classes' from an obstacle into a parametrisation: hard primes come with extra representations.
first_step: For Mordell-hard primes ≤ 10⁷, compute representations by forms of discriminants dividing −4·840 and correlate (x, y) with known certificates (u, B, C).
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Euler-system-style bounds on the 'obstruction group' of certificate-free levels
connection: Kolyvagin bounded Selmer groups with an Euler system of Heegner points. Define for p the 'obstruction group' O_p = set of levels/windows that fail with their local data; a norm-compatible system of near-certificates across levels (if it existed) would bound O_p and force it to be smaller than the set of all levels.
why: Highly speculative, but Euler systems are the one tool that converts a supply of compatible objects into a bound on an obstruction.
first_step: First check whether near-certificates at levels C | C′ satisfy any norm/trace compatibility (e.g. divisor classes mod 4C′ reducing to classes mod 4C).

title: Rédei-type reciprocity explains T1 — look for its 'higher' analogues in ES sub-routes
connection: Negative Pell's obstructions beyond local ones come from Rédei symbols (higher reciprocity). T1 is a quadratic-reciprocity cancellation. Search for Rédei-symbol-type (quartic/biquadratic) conditions that predict extra failures of sub-routes ((★), b=1, ES₅) among primes, beyond what the BM/genus layer explains.
why: If found, such conditions refine the main term (like Stevenhagen's refinement) and sharpen targets; if absent, the genus layer is complete.
first_step: Compute Rédei symbols [a, b, p] for small a, b and correlate with (★) failures / low counts.

title: Congruence mod ℓ from a mod-ℓ Galois image: ES counts with large-image structure
connection: Swinnerton-Dyer's classification of exceptional primes for τ gives congruences τ(p) ≡ explicit function of p (mod ℓ). If ES counts (or a weighted combination of level series, Thm K) were coefficients of a form with a mod-ℓ Galois representation, congruences R(p) ≡ g(p) (mod ℓ) would follow, and ES would hold wherever g(p) ≢ 0.
why: Turns ES non-vanishing into a congruence problem with explicit exceptions — the τ approach.
first_step: Check whether the theta-quotient/Eisenstein parts of Thm K have coefficients satisfying Eisenstein-type congruences mod small ℓ (they are divisor sums twisted by characters, so congruences like σ_χ(N) ≡ … mod ℓ may exist).

title: Jacobi-symbol parity forces a prime factor in a nonresidue class — how far toward the exact class?
connection: Elkies: (−D/H_D(j)) parity forces a prime factor inert in ℚ(√−D). ES windows: (N_e/e) = (p/e) for N_e = (p+e)/4, so if (p/e) = −1 then N_e has a prime factor q with (q/e) = −1 (FORCED_WINDOW's condition). ES needs more: a divisor ratio exactly ≡ −1. Identify what extra 'forcing' (higher-order characters, sign/size of N_e) could pin the class.
why: Clarifies the gap between the proven quadratic forcing and the needed exact-class statement; Elkies needed only a quadratic class.
first_step: For window primes e ≡ 3 (mod 4) with (p/e) = −1, measure the distribution of the forced nonresidue factors' classes and how often a complementary divisor completes −1.

title: Two-candidate version: (★) and b=1 as Heath-Brown's 'one of three' with two
connection: Heath-Brown's argument needs three candidates because two can both fail. ES data show (★) and b=1 never fail together ≤ 10⁸; test whether a third family (e.g. ES₅, small windows) is needed to make a proof-style argument robust, by finding primes where any two of three fail.
why: Determines the minimal number of families an 'at least one works' argument must juggle.
first_step: Compute joint failure sets of (★), b=1, ES₅ and the first-k windows up to 10⁹; report pairs/triples that fail together.
refs: Heath-Brown, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986) 27-38 (Artin's conjecture for primitive roots)

title: Supersingular points and maximal orders: ≈ p/12 objects attached to every p
connection: Every prime p has ≈ p/12 supersingular j-invariants, in bijection (Deuring) with left ideal classes of a fixed maximal order of the quaternion algebra ramified at p and ∞ (maximal-order types correspond to j up to Frobenius conjugation). These always exist, like Elkies's CM values; map them (or their small-norm elements, Eichler orientations) to ES certificate data.
why: Supplies power-many canonical objects for every p; if any natural map lands in certificates with positive probability, existence follows from their number.
first_step: Read the repo's supersingular/Eichler memos; for small p compute the maximal orders' reduced norms forms and test whether ES certificates appear as small vectors.

title: Kaplansky-type ternary forms with conditional (GRH) complete lists as structural analogues
connection: Beyond Ramanujan's form, several ternary forms have GRH-conditional complete lists of exceptions (Ono–Soundararajan type). Their exception lists are finite but sporadic; ES-adjacent statements with sporadic exceptions (U(n) list, b=1 failures) might be 'ternary-form-like'. Test whether the U(n)/b=1 exceptions are represented/non-represented by specific ternary forms.
why: A direct dictionary between sporadic ES-adjacent exceptions and ternary-form exceptions would import Waldspurger/GRH technology.
first_step: For the known sporadic exception lists, test representability by all reduced positive ternary forms of discriminant ≤ 500.

title: Syracuse-type random variable for ES: the 2-adic/3-adic structure of minimal certificates
connection: Tao's Collatz proof analysed the distribution of a 3-adic 'Syracuse random variable'. ES certificates carry 2-adic data (4 | t; 8ℤ − p branch) and 3-adic data (Mordell classes mod 3). Define the analogous random variable (residues of minimal certificate parameters mod 2^k, 3^k) and study its distribution and mixing as p varies.
why: Fine-scale mixing of certificate residues is the kind of statement that powers almost-all → 'almost every scale' improvements.
first_step: Compute the distribution of minimal certificate parameters mod 2^k·3^j over primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for Fourier decay.
refs: arXiv:1909.03562 (Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values)

title: Function-field large sieve on the ES certificate set (Hsu-type FF large sieve)
connection: The FF large sieve is sharp with explicit constants. Applied to 'P avoiding all certificate classes for moduli ≤ Q', it bounds the FF exceptional set; Z has the same inequality with worse explicit constants.
why: The FF large-sieve bound can be compared directly with the FF exceptional count computed exactly, calibrating how lossy the Z large-sieve route is.
first_step: Compute the FF large-sieve prediction for q=3, A=T, deg ≤ 12 and compare with the exact failure counts in data/ffl.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Katz monodromy for Kloosterman/Salié-type sums in ES Type II counts at q → ∞
connection: Type II counts at fixed P are sums of incomplete Kloosterman/Salié-like sums; over F_q[T] with q→∞, Katz's equidistribution gives square-root cancellation with known monodromy groups.
why: If the relevant monodromy is computed, it predicts the fluctuation law of the fixed-p count over Z (Katz–Sarnak style) and so the lower-tail behaviour.
first_step: Identify the exact exponential sum in the FF Type II count (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §4) and look up its geometric monodromy in Katz 'Gauss sums, Kloosterman sums and monodromy groups'.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Chowla over F_q[T] (proved for large q) ↔ parity barrier in ES sieve arguments
connection: ES lower-bound sieves hit the parity barrier; FF Chowla (Sawin–Shusterman, large q) breaks parity in FF. If an FF ES statement follows from FF Chowla, the integer statement needs a Chowla-type input.
why: Clarifies whether parity is the precise barrier for a sieve proof of ES.
first_step: Check whether the FF ES counting function at fixed P can be written with a Möbius/Liouville twist that Chowla controls.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Denominators in short intervals (Croot) ↔ size windows for ES solutions
connection: Croot studied unit fractions with denominators in short intervals [N, N + N^θ]. ES solutions have x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4] and y, z in structured ranges; asking for all three denominators in a short window is a size-constrained world.
why: Size windows are central to the repo's window/slice analysis; Croot's techniques give existence for long sums, hinting at what's needed for three.
first_step: Read Croot math/9904181 to see whether his argument has a 3-term component; compute the window widths of ES solutions for hard primes.

title: Derived-set (accumulation) structure: 4/n is never an accumulation point of 3-term sums except via 2-term limits
connection: The set E₃ of 3-term sums is closed with accumulation points in E₂ (2-term sums). 4/n ∈ E₃ is a statement about an isolated vs limit point.
why: If 4/n lies in the closure of E₃ for trivial reasons (approximations from above/below), quantifying the approximation rate may force membership for arithmetic reasons.
first_step: Compute dist(4/p, E₃ ∖ {4/p}) for p ≤ 10^4 and compare with the expected spacing.

title: Modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 (mod p) with X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (mod t) and XY = tp+1
connection: Words ↔ points (X,Y) = (A, A*) on the modular hyperbola XY ≡ 1 mod p with X, Y ≡ −1 mod t and the exact archimedean condition XY = tp+1. Shparlinski's survey covers point counts in boxes via Kloosterman sums.
why: Native results give points of XY ≡ c mod m in boxes of side ≥ m^{1/2+ε}. ES needs a hyperbola-shaped region (XY exactly tp+1), and that shape is the whole difficulty.
first_step: Compute the fraction of integral Type II hyperbola points in each mod-4cd class and compare with the modular hyperbola's equidistribution.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0076] From Shparlinski's survey, locate the best result on modular-hyperbola points in hyperbolic (not box) regions and see what size it requires.
[analogues-0213] Map one ES slice exactly to a modular-hyperbola box problem and compare required box size with the Weil-bound threshold.
[free_fable-0016] Read Shparlinski's survey 'Modular hyperbolas' §'points with restricted coordinates'; check whether divisor-restricted hyperbola points are addressed anywhere.
[free_opus-0371] Read Shparlinski, 'Modular hyperbolas' (arXiv:1103.2879; Jpn. J. Math. 2012) and list results about points with coordinates restricted to divisor sets.
refs: Shparlinski, Modular hyperbolas, Japan. J. Math. 7 (2012)

title: Least quadratic non-residue (Burgess/Vinogradov) ↔ least ES certificate
connection: ES certificates are found by searching small parameters (e.g. least C with 4Cp + 1 having a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C). The least quadratic non-residue problem has a GRH bound O(log² p) and unconditional p^{1/(4√e)}.
why: If the least certificate behaves like the least non-residue, ES is implied by a GRH-type character-sum bound — exactly where the repo's EXSET_LINNIK memos look.
first_step: Compute the least certificate parameter C(p) for p ≤ 10^7 and compare its growth with log² p; check EXSET_LINNIK.md.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0188] Write the certificate indicator as a combination of characters mod moduli of size ≤ p^θ and check whether short character sum bounds could give existence for θ < 1 (probably fails due to tied moduli — record precisely where).

title: Two-prime world: ES for n = pq simultaneously with prescribed distribution of p, q among denominators
connection: ES(pq) is implied by ES(p), but asking that p | x and q | y (split) is a constrained world that couples two primes. Its failures are pairs (p, q) — a 2-dimensional exceptional set.
why: 2D exceptional sets can be studied with bilinear methods (sums over p and q), sometimes yielding results unavailable in 1D.
first_step: Compute split-solvability for p, q ≡ 1 mod 4 below 500; see if failures form a structured set (e.g. both in square classes).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Bounded-slice world: ES with e = 4x − p ≤ E fixed — false for each fixed E (Mordell), find growth of needed E
connection: For fixed E, the union of slices e ≤ E is a finite covering by congruence classes, so fails at square classes. The least E(p) is the true complexity measure; ES ⇔ E(p) < ∞.
why: Bounds on E(p) like O(log^A p) would be a precise and plausible (GRH-like) target; repo memos study it.
first_step: Compute E(p) to 10^7 and fit growth; compare with the least-certificate item.

title: Zeta-function world: Dirichlet series Σ_n #ES(n) n^{−s} and its analytic continuation
connection: If the generating Dirichlet series of ES counts has a meromorphic continuation with a pole structure (Elsholtz–Tao give average order), its behaviour near s = 1 encodes average counts; zero-free regions control exceptions.
why: A Dirichlet series with an Euler-product-like factorization would turn ES counting into L-function theory (repo: anal_dirichlet_series).
first_step: Pointer: read BRAINSTORM/anal_dirichlet_series.md; compute the series' local factors numerically.

title: ES modulo p with denominators in an interval [1, H] (Shparlinski-type small solutions)
connection: Count solutions of 4/n ≡ 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (mod p) with 1 ≤ x, y, z ≤ H. For H ≥ p^{1/2+ε} character-sum bounds give many solutions; ES-type statements need H ~ p^{1/3}-ish lifts (the real solutions have x ≈ p/4 though).
why: Determines the minimal box H(p) for modular solvability; integer ES solutions give boxes of size p² for z, so this is a different (stronger) finite question, but its methods (Kloosterman) are those relevant to Type II slices.
first_step: Compute H(p) numerically for p ≤ 2000 and compare with p^{1/3}, p^{1/2}.

title: Beatty-restricted denominators: 4/n = Σ 1/⌊k_iθ⌋ for irrational θ
connection: Restricting denominators to a Beatty sequence (density 1/θ) is a 'quasi-random' thinning with equidistribution available (Weyl sums). The world sits between ES (θ = 1) and random thinning.
why: Equidistribution makes the Beatty world analytically tractable on average; if heuristics predict a threshold θ_c beyond which failures appear, it calibrates the ES lottery.
first_step: For θ ∈ {√2, φ, e/2} test p ≤ 5000 for Beatty-restricted ES; record failure counts.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Lifting from mod-p solutions: Hensel/approximation world 'ES over Z/p^kZ with archimedean box'
connection: A solution mod p^k with representatives in the box (p/4, 3p/4] × [1, p²] × [1, p³] and k large enough is an integer solution (the equation is exact once p^k exceeds the size). So ES ⇔ a box-solution modulo a large modulus.
why: Recasts ES as a box problem in a finite ring where character-sum methods apply; the box is tiny relative to the modulus, which is why it's hard.
first_step: Quantify: the box volume vs modulus at which heuristics predict a solution (= log²p expected count); compare with known small-solution theorems.

title: Max-plus/min-plus degeneration families (Maslov dequantization): ES_h for h → 0
connection: Deform 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n via x ↦ x^{1/h}-type dequantization; as h → 0 the equation becomes a tropical (max-plus) relation of exponents. Intermediate h give real-analytic families connecting ES to its tropical limit.
why: Mostly geometric intuition (size windows); may help visualize which size patterns are forced.
first_step: Low priority; note.

title: Sato–Tate-type world: distribution of ES solution 'angles' (x/p, y/p², …) as p varies
connection: Normalized solution coordinates (x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4], log y/log p, …) may equidistribute w.r.t. a limiting measure as p → ∞, like Sato–Tate angles. Hard primes would be those whose solutions avoid the bulk of the measure.
why: A limiting measure gives a precise heuristic for the probability that no solution falls in the 'admissible region' — the ES lower-tail question.
first_step: For p < 2·10^4 histogram x/p over all solutions and test convergence of the empirical measure.

title: Least prime in an arithmetic progression (Linnik) vs least certificate level
connection: ES certificates at level C are prime-free (divisors, not primes), but the simplest certificates use a prime q ≡ 3 mod 4 with (p/q) = −1 or similar. Linnik's constant controls the least such prime.
why: The least-QNR and Linnik problems are the archetypal 'pointwise thin existence' theorems in NT, and the repo uses Burgess for the BM main term.
first_step: Calibration: compare least ES certificate level with ℓ(p) (least prime with (p/ℓ) = −1) for p ≤ 10⁹; is the certificate level ≤ C·ℓ(p)^κ?
alt_first_steps: [signature-0451] Formulate a 'log-free zero density' statement for the family {χ_{−4uB}} that would imply min level C ≪ p^ε, and check what is known.

title: Littlewood conjecture / Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss measure rigidity for product approximations
connection: EKL: the exceptional set for Littlewood's conjecture has dimension 0, via measure rigidity of diagonal actions; ES approximates 4/n by sums of unit fractions — a multiplicative Diophantine approximation shape.
why: Diagonal-action rigidity controls simultaneous multiplicative approximations, the structure of 4/n − 1/x ≈ product-type quantities.
first_step: Check whether ES's second step (4/n − 1/x = 1/y + 1/z) can be phrased as a multiplicative approximation problem for a diagonal action.
refs: Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss, Invariant measures and the set of exceptions to Littlewood's conjecture, Ann. Math. 164 (2006)

title: Feature: power-size witness reservoir
connection: Dividing-line feature 'power-size witness reservoir'. ES LACKS it (expected witnesses ≍ log² p). To supply it one could: embed ES(p) in a 4-term problem 4/p = Σ_{i≤4} 1/x_i (power count) and prove a 'merging' rule that converts a structured 4-term solution into a 3-term one
why: Every proved pointwise result with polylog witnesses (Linnik–Gallagher, Chen) rides on a power reservoir.
first_step: Count 4-term solutions of 4/p with one denominator in a prescribed divisor class and test how often a merge (1/a + 1/b = 1/c) is available.

title: Feature: free (untied) witness parameter
connection: Dividing-line feature 'free (untied) witness parameter'. ES has a partially free parameter C (4Cp+1) but the modulus 4C moves with it (B2). To supply it one could: freeze the modulus: restrict to C in a fixed finite set and use many p-tied integers simultaneously (fixed-modulus character events, F3)
why: Least-witness theorems under GRH need fixed moduli; ES's moving modulus is the precise lack.
first_step: List fixed-modulus sub-events of ES (C fixed) and compute the fraction of p ≡ 1 mod 24 solved by C ≤ 10 — how many fixed C are needed empirically?

title: Feature: root-number / parity forcing
connection: Dividing-line feature 'root-number / parity forcing'. ES LACKS a parity-forced object. To supply it one could: attach an L-function or Selmer group to p (e.g. from a genus-one fibre of the ES surface) whose root number is −1 for all p ≡ 1 mod 24
why: Parity of Selmer ranks proves 100% results (Smith) and conditional pointwise results (BSD).
first_step: For the elliptic fibrations of the ES surface over Q(p), compute root numbers of a few fibres for p ≡ 1 mod 24 and see whether a sign is forced.

title: Feature: exceptional set has a canonical shape (AP / squares / sparse algebraic)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'exceptional set has a canonical shape (AP / squares / sparse algebraic)'. ES HAS one canonical bad shape (odd squares, T1) and sporadic U(n) values. To supply it one could: prove that ES failures, if any, avoid every other structured shape (polynomial values, Crocker-type sparse families, APs)
why: Proved/failed problems both display structured exception sets; classifying admissible exception shapes narrows disproof routes.
first_step: Check ES numerically on dense structured families: p = a²+1, p = 2^k·m+1, p = Fermat-like numbers up to large sizes; record min R(p)/log² p per family.

title: Feature: Siegel-ineffective finite exceptions
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Siegel-ineffective finite exceptions'. ES COULD HAVE (U(n) sporadic list looks like idoneal / Ramanujan-form lists). To supply it one could: identify an L-function or class number whose smallness would control U(n) failures; prove finiteness ineffectively
why: Idoneal numbers and Ramanujan's form show 'finite + ineffective' is the natural outcome for class-number-governed problems.
first_step: Factor the U(n) sporadic list and compute class numbers of Q(√−n), Q(√−4n), Q(√−3n) etc.; look for uniformly small values.

title: Feature: effectivity of known partial results
connection: Dividing-line feature 'effectivity of known partial results'. ES Vaughan-type bounds are effective; no ineffective input in sight. To supply it one could: allow ineffective inputs (Siegel zeros) — maybe a dichotomy: either no Siegel zero ⇒ ES for p ≫ 1, or Siegel zero ⇒ ES via Deuring–Heilbronn
why: Some pointwise results (ternary forms, Linnik) are proved via Deuring–Heilbronn dichotomies.
first_step: Check whether a Siegel zero would help ES (exceptional character makes primes ≡ some class rare — helps or hurts divisor-in-class events?).

title: Between: ES with the minimal denominator bounded: x ≤ p/4 + p^θ
connection: Linnik-constant analogue: max over p of minimal admissible window.
why: If the minimal x always lies in a short window, ES becomes a bounded search (Π₁ → decidable per p with explicit bound).
first_step: Compute max_{p ≤ 10^9} (x_min(p) − ⌈p/4⌉)/log² p and fit.

title: ES as an infinite congruence 'covering' of the non-squares; distortion-method analysis
connection: Hough and Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba bound the uncovered density of covering systems via a distorted-measure sieve. ES Type II (★): the classes p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) over all (u,B) must cover every prime; they never cover odd squares (T1). Study the uncovered set of the subsystem with moduli ≤ M within [1, X] as M grows.
why: The distortion method controls the uncovered set precisely for systems with many moduli; ES's system is explicit and its uncovered set is known to contain squares.
first_step: Compute the uncovered set of {−(u+B) mod 4uB : 4uB ≤ M} in [1, X] for M up to 10⁵, X up to 10⁸; compare its size with #squares + #(small sporadic) and track how fast non-squares disappear.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0186] Search literature for 'infinite covering systems primes divergent sum of reciprocals' and for Hough/Balister lemmas about uncovered sets under divergent density.
[signature-0065] Compute the density δ_C of primes covered by level C alone and Σ_C δ_C up to C ≤ 10³; compare with the BBMST criterion.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))
unverified: Hough 2015, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems (Annals 181)

title: Feature: witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'witness = divisor in a class (multiplicative) rather than prime value (additive)'. ES HAS multiplicative witnesses; parity barrier is not obviously relevant. To supply it one could: use multiplicative-function machinery (Halász, Matomäki–Radziwiłł) on indicator-type functions of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'
why: Problems with prime-valued witnesses hit the parity barrier; divisor-in-class problems are governed by Stewart-type subgroup criteria instead.
first_step: Express 1[N has a divisor ≡ −1 mod q] in terms of characters of (ℤ/q)^× via the subgroup criterion and check if Halász-type bounds apply when N runs over 4Cp+1, C ≤ X.

title: Feature: Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Linnik-constant bound (smallest witness ≤ n^A)'. ES UNKNOWN for ES; known witnesses are small in practice. To supply it one could: prove a conditional (GRH) bound on the smallest certificate parameter, turning ES into a finite check per p
why: Least-witness theorems (Linnik, Bach) are among the few pointwise polylog results, though conditional.
first_step: Compute max over p ≤ 10^9 of the minimal Type I parameter a·d (or C) and compare with log² p.

title: Transfer: ES as a Linnik-type problem in the progression 1 mod 4p
connection: For fixed p the auxiliary integers N_C = 4Cp + 1 run through the AP 1 (mod 4p) indexed by C; ES (Type I) asks for an element N_C with a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C. This is a 'least element of an AP with a factorisation property' question, like Linnik's least prime in an AP.
why: Linnik-type theorems are pointwise in the modulus 4p (power reservoir of AP elements up to (4p)^L) — but the required class mod 4C moves with C, the B2 feature.
first_step: Count, for p ≤ 10^6, the least C with a valid divisor and compare with log² p and with the least prime ≡ 1 mod 4p; check whether 'C ≤ p^ε' always holds.

title: Transfer: Maynard–Tao tuples of C's
connection: Choose C ∈ {C₀h₁, …, C₀h_k} admissible and force many N_{C_i} = 4C_i p + 1 to be almost-prime simultaneously, then use the multiplicative relations between them to force a class −1 factor.
why: Multi-dimensional sieves produce simultaneous structure; ES needs one success among many correlated shifted integers.
first_step: Check whether the N_{C_i} with C_i = C₀h_i (fixed p) form an admissible linear tuple in the variable C₀.

title: Transfer: Duke equidistribution for represented values
connection: As d grows, values of forms of discriminant −4d (Heegner-type points) equidistribute (Duke 1988); this might equidistribute the residues −f mod 4ad that Type I offers.
why: Equidistribution in d at fixed p would give many independent chances; pointwise in p requires equidistribution uniform in a small window of d.
first_step: Check the error terms in Duke's theorem vs the window of d needed (d ≤ log^A p).

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for 'no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)'
connection: For C = 1, 'N has no divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)' iff all odd prime factors of N are ≡ 1 (mod 4): a half-dimensional sifted set (Landau–Ramanujan). For general C, ES failure at N requires the prime factors of N to avoid generating −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: The semi-linear sieve gives sharp upper and lower bounds for such sifted sets; summing over C at fixed p could bound the failure probability.
first_step: For fixed p, compute #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C} and compare with the semi-linear sieve prediction ∏(1 − 1/ℓ)^{1/2}-type density.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0203] Formulate the upper-bound sieve problem: #{C ≤ X : N_C is H_C-confined} ≤ ? and see whether the expected X·(log)^{−1/2} type bound is attainable pointwise.

[translate-0079] Write the failure at fixed C as 'all divisors avoid −1 mod 4C' (stronger than a prime-factor condition); quantify with the half-dimensional sieve over C ≤ log p and check the expected joint-failure density.
refs: Iwaniec, The half dimensional sieve (Acta Arith. 1976)

title: Transfer: Halász / Matomäki–Radziwiłł for confinement indicators
connection: The indicator that N has all prime factors in H ⊂ (ℤ/q)^× is multiplicative in N; Halász-type theorems give mean values over short intervals / sequences.
why: Pointwise confinement over the sequence N_C (C ≤ X) is a mean of a multiplicative function along an AP 1 mod 4p — Matomäki–Radziwiłł style results along APs may bound it.
first_step: Check whether MR-type results apply to multiplicative functions along APs with modulus as large as 4p and length X ≈ p^θ.

title: Feature: variance / second moment control
connection: Dividing-line feature 'variance / second moment control'. ES KNOWN on average (Elsholtz–Tao moments). To supply it one could: use the second moment Σ_p R(p)² with Cauchy–Schwarz pointwise in short families (primes in a residue class mod a large modulus)
why: Romanoff-type and almost-all results come from second moments; pointwise needs higher moments or rigidity.
first_step: Read Elsholtz–Tao's moment computations; check whether higher moments (k-th) are computed.

title: Feature: uniformity in an auxiliary large parameter
connection: Dividing-line feature 'uniformity in an auxiliary large parameter'. ES PARTIAL (PW uniform-in-m Vaughan bound). To supply it one could: introduce an artificial large parameter (m, or modulus Q of restricted classes) where uniform results give pointwise results at a special point
why: Function-field large-q results and PW's uniformity show how an extra parameter can be leveraged.
first_step: Ask: is ES(p) implied by a uniform-in-m statement for m/(kp) with k varying (scaling ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn))?

title: Feature: structure of the exceptional set at composite n
connection: Dividing-line feature 'structure of the exceptional set at composite n'. ES ES at composites reduces to prime factors (trivial). To supply it one could: use the fact that U(n)-type variants have sporadic composite failures (105 = 3·5·7, …) to locate which sub-certificate families matter
why: Composite sporadic failures of variants show which certificate families are 'load-bearing'.
first_step: Factor U(n) sporadic list and check whether each prime factor's variant certificates are 'incompatible' under scaling.

title: Feature: strong cancellation in a fixed-target character sum (Rickards–Stange)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'strong cancellation in a fixed-target character sum (Rickards–Stange)'. ES LACKS (fibre size log²). To supply it one could: replace the fibre over p by a larger fibre over a p-dependent family (e.g. all n = p·k, k ≤ K) of size power, then extract p
why: The only proved 'squares + sporadic' theorem uses a long character sum over one target's fibre.
first_step: Count solutions of 4/(pk) over k ≤ K that do NOT come from scaling — is that fibre power-size and does it carry p-information?

title: Sieve-limit (parity-type) model for ES
connection: Selberg's parity example shows sieves cannot distinguish primes from integers with λ(n) = −1. Ask for an analogue: a set S with the sieve statistics of primes (level of distribution, local densities) on which every ES certificate family fails — odd squares are such a set for certificate lines (T1).
why: If such a model exists, sieve-only proofs of ES are impossible; if the statistics of primes already exclude it, a sieve route exists.
first_step: Try S = {n : n ≡ 1 mod 24, n = m² or m²·(unit-like)} and generalisations; check which sieve axioms each candidate violates.

title: Analogy with Lehmer's question for unit fractions: smallest positive value of 4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z
connection: If ES fails at p, the closest approach |4/p − Σ 1/x_i| > 0 is bounded below by 1/(pxyz). Study the 'Egyptian approximation gap' distribution; ES ⇔ gap = 0 is attained.
why: Converts existence into a Diophantine-approximation statement where Baker/geometry-of-numbers tools might bite.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^5, the minimal positive gap and the number of near-solutions with gap ≤ 1/(p·xyz)·K.

title: Result: least certificate-family size s(p) has a p-independent distribution (median 22, 99% ≤ ~200) and the CRT model predicts its maximum
connection: For all 179 468 hard-class primes p < 10⁸ the least s = ad (Type I) or ab (Type II) solving p has median 22, 90% quantile 86, 99% quantile 209 — identical to the < 10⁷ sample (22, 85, 187). The max over p < 10⁷ is 1133 (model n·δ(X) = 1 predicts ≈ 1210); over p < 10⁸ it is 2814 at p = 53049049 (model ≈ 1990, next-largest 1467).
why: Quantifies 'how far' one must search per prime and shows the independence model is calibrated on the extreme-value statistic, not only on averages. EVIDENCE only.
first_step: Push to 10⁹ (≈ 1.6·10⁶ hard primes, model predicts max ≈ 3·10³) and check the record-setters for near-square structure (cf. NEAR_SQUARE.md).

title: Prediction: least ES family size grows like exp((ln x / c)^{1/3}) — super-polylog, sub-power
connection: If δ(X) ≈ exp(−c (ln X)³), the largest least-family size among hard primes ≤ x is ≈ exp((ln π_hard(x)/c)^{1/3}) ≈ exp(((ln x)/c)^{1/3}): about 5·10⁴ at x = 10¹⁸. This matches the shape of H4_NOT_POLYLOG.md's proven lower bounds exp((log p)^κ), κ < 1/12 (κ < 1/6 relative to (G)), and suggests κ = 1/3 is the true exponent (for this coordinate).
why: Gives a concrete conjectural Linnik-constant law for ES and an explicit target for the proven-lower-bound programme (raise κ towards 1/3) and for any upper bound (which would be ES-strength).
first_step: Compare with the Salez / Mihnea–Dumitru verification data to 10¹⁸ if family sizes are recorded there; check whether the H4 coordinate and s(p) are comparable.

title: Connection: ES ⟺ Frobenius of p lies in a union of Chebotarev sets of growing level — least-prime-in-Chebotarev theory in reverse
connection: Each certificate family is a Chebotarev condition in Q(ζ_{4ad}) (splitting/residue condition). ES says Frob_p always lands in the union over all levels. Least-prime results answer 'is the first prime in a fixed Chebotarev set small?'; ES asks 'is every prime in the union of growing sets?'.
why: A 'reverse Chebotarev covering' framing makes the dividing feature precise: unions over growing level with total density → 1 at rate exp(−c log³ X).
first_step: Search for theorems of the form 'every prime p lies in some Chebotarev set C_L with L ≤ f(p)' for natural families (e.g. every p splits completely in some field of a family).

title: Connection: 'every prime splits in some member of a family of fields' problems
connection: Examples: every prime p is ≡ 1 mod some small prime ℓ (trivial), every p is a QNR mod some small ℓ (least non-residue), every p splits in some Q(√d) with d small (least QR prime). ES is a non-abelian-free but class-valued version.
why: These 'some member of a family' problems are proved pointwise exactly when the family has a forced member (Burgess / pigeonhole); identifying the forced member is the crux.
first_step: List such problems with their least-witness bounds and check which have unconditional polylog/power bounds.

title: Connection: Erdős–Hall 'every n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m for some small m'-type statements
connection: Stewart's criterion makes 'n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m' central. Ask the pointwise question 'for every n ≡ 1 mod 4p…'; the analogous unconditional results for integers in APs are about divisors in residue classes (Erdős–Hall, Hall–Tenenbaum).
why: Divisor-in-class problems for individual integers are typically almost-all; pointwise results need structure (e.g. n has many prime factors).
first_step: Literature check: 'divisors in residue classes Hall Tenenbaum individual integers'.

title: Connection: residue model vs actual primes — the only gap is size, not residue
connection: Type I/II parametrisations have no size constraint (Pomerance slides): the residue model is EXACT for each fixed family set. ES ⟺ no prime survives all families; the gap between the model and ES is that X must grow with p (and Chebotarev error terms in level ≈ exp((log p)^{1/3})).
why: Reformulates ES as a uniform Chebotarev/sieve problem at level exp((log p)^{1/3+ε}): far below power level, where Bombieri–Vinogradov-type averages are strong — but needed pointwise for one p.
first_step: Check: is there any pointwise result 'every prime p avoids a sieve of level L = exp((log p)^θ) only if p is in an explicit thin set'? (Least-witness theory for sieves.)

title: Large sieve inequality applied to the exceptional set with the C-form classes as the sifting classes
connection: Classical large sieve: if a set S ⊂ [1, X] avoids ω(q) residue classes mod q for each q ≤ Q, then |S| ≤ (X + Q²)/L with L = Σ_{q ≤ Q} μ²(q) Π_{p|q} ω(p)/(p − ω(p)). For the C-form, S = exceptional set avoids, for each prime a ≡ −1 (mod 4C), the single class r_{C,a} mod a — ω(a) = #{C : 4C | a + 1} = τ((a+1)/4)-ish. So L ≈ Σ_{a ≤ Q} #{C: 4C | a+1}/a ≈ Σ_a τ((a+1)/4)/a ≈ (1/2) log²Q. Hence |exceptions ≤ X| ≪ (X + Q²)/log²Q — with Q = √X: ≪ X/log²X. A quick, elementary exceptional-set bound; weaker than Vaughan but *structurally* it shows the exceptional set has density 0 with a log² saving that mirrors the log²p count.
why: Elementary, and its proof shape (large sieve with ω(a) ~ τ(a+1)) might extend to a *weighted* large sieve giving more; and it exhibits ES's exceptional-set bounds as a special case of sieving by 'divisor-many' classes.
first_step: Verify the computation of L carefully (sum over prime a only, or all a via the full large sieve with multiplicative ω); compare with Vaughan's exp(−c(log N)^{2/3}); check whether larger Q (via Montgomery–Vaughan with Q up to X^{1/2}) or Type II's extra (c,d) classes improve the exponent.
alt_first_steps: [dividing-0328] Derive the model's exceptional-set prediction: #{p ≤ x unsolved by families ≤ X(x)} ≈ π(x)·δ(X); optimise X under level-of-distribution constraints.
[tools-0255] Recheck which large-sieve inequality the 3/4-exponent note uses and whether Gallagher's larger sieve (prime-power moduli) gives more.
refs: Montgomery, 'The analytic principle of the large sieve' (1978)
Gallagher, A larger sieve, Acta Arith. 18 (1971)

title: log U(p) ≈ const − 0.30·log L_Q(1,χ_p), saturating at Q ≈ 30
connection: Adding log of the truncated Euler product ∏_{q≤Q}(1−χ_p(q)/q)^{−1} to the (log p, loglog p) regression gives α ≈ −0.30 and R²-gain 0.29 (Q=2), 0.40 (Q=3), 0.47 (Q=7), 0.49 (Q=31), 0.48 (Q=1000).
why: About half the residual variance of log U(p) is explained by the quadratic character of p at primes ≤ 30; this suggests (it does not prove) that much of the count's fluctuation is governed by finitely many local data.
first_step: Fit with separate coefficients per small prime q (2,3,5,7,11,13) to get the local weights; compare to the Elsholtz–Tao local densities.

title: U(p) vs τ(p−1) and σ(p−1)/(p−1): ρ ≈ −0.53
connection: More divisors of p−1 ⇒ fewer ES solutions (ρ(τ(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) = −0.53, ρ(φ(p−1)/(p−1)) = +0.42).
why: Smooth p−1 means p ≡ 1 modulo many small numbers — the Mordell-class obstruction; links ES hardness to the Erdős–Pomerance world of smooth shifted primes.
first_step: Test whether τ(p−1) remains significant after controlling for L(1,χ_p) (partial correlation).

title: U(p) vs τ((p+3)/4): ρ = +0.59
connection: U(p) residual correlates +0.59 with τ((p+3)/4) and +0.48 with τ(p+3), but only +0.12 with τ(4p+1), +0.12 with τ(p+4), +0.05 with τ(p+12).
why: x = (p+3)/4 is the smallest admissible first denominator; solutions with x=(p+3)/4 come from divisors of (p+3)/4-related numbers; a single shift explains a large share of variance.
first_step: Count solutions by x−⌈p/4⌉ ∈ {0,1,2,…} and measure what fraction of U(p) comes from the first few x; relate to divisors of p+3, p+7, …

title: U(p) mod m is equidistributed (small bias at U ≡ 1 mod 6)
connection: For p≡1(4) >100 (n=8 843), U(p) mod 2,3,4,8 are flat within noise; U(p) ≡ 1 (mod 6) is 1361 vs ≈1490 expected (≈3.5σ low).
why: No parity constraint ⇒ no simple involution explains U(p); the mod-6 dip may be a counting artefact (e.g. solutions with y=z).
first_step: Separate solutions with repeated denominators (x=y or y=z) and recount mod 6.

title: m/p failures are enriched in primes adjacent to 5-smooth numbers
connection: For m=12, 15 of 22 failures have p−1 or p+1 5-smooth (only 182 such primes ≤ 10⁵ in total); m=20: 27/63; m=24: 39/146 — OEIS returns spurious A219669 ('primes neighboring a 5-smooth number') for m=45.
why: Primes next to smooth numbers are ≡ ±1 modulo many small numbers simultaneously — the Mordell-class mechanism; a quantitative version is a 'smooth-neighbour' hardness law.
first_step: Compute failure rate among 5-smooth-neighbour primes vs others for each m; extend to 7-smooth.

title: Mean R(n)/log²n on n ≡ 1 (4) drifts 0.145 → 0.133 (10³ → 10⁶)
connection: Average of R(n)/(log n)² over n ≡ 1 (4) in [X, 2X]: 0.1446 (10³), 0.1388 (10⁴), 0.1353 (10⁵), 0.1332 (10⁶); FRONTIER lists constants 1/8 = 0.125 (all integers) and 3/(2π²) = 0.152.
why: Drift towards 1/8 with a 1/log correction is a sharp numerical test of the second-order term in the (★) mean.
first_step: Fit mean = 1/8 + a/log X + b/log²X to 10⁸; compare with a second-order term from the divisor-sum asymptotics.

title: U(p) residual vs Σ_{d≤8} τ(p+4d) is null (ρ = +0.02)
connection: The b = 1 (López Type A) line asks for a divisor of p+4d ≡ −1 (mod 4d); yet the raw divisor mass Σ_{d≤8} τ(p+4d) is uncorrelated with U(p), while τ((p+3)/4) correlates +0.59.
why: Divisor *mass* of shifts is not what matters — the residue-class restriction is; shows why naive divisor-sum lower bounds don't track solvability.
first_step: Replace τ by the class-restricted count #{e | p+4d : e ≡ −1 (4d)} and recompute.

title: τ(p+1) and τ(p+4) correlate weakly (+0.12), τ(p+12) not at all
connection: Shifted divisor functions at shifts 1,4,12 carry little information on ES count, unlike shift 3 (+0.48 for τ(p+3)).
why: Highlights the special role of the shift 3 (x = (p+3)/4), i.e. the first greedy step, among all shifts.
first_step: Tabulate ρ(U, τ(p+s)) for s = 1..50 to find the full 'shift spectrum' and compare with which x-values carry solutions.

title: Root numbers / L-functions of quadratic twists of 32a1 by p
connection: Compute-and-check: the twist E^{(p)}: py² = x³ − x (congruent-number-type curve) has root number determined by p mod 8; its analytic rank at hard primes vs others.
why: Congruent-number style curves are the classic 'Diophantine via elliptic curves' fingerprint; ES hardness clustered in p ≡ 1 (8) where these twists have root number +1.
first_step: Use pari ellanalyticrank on twists for p ≡ 1 (8) ≤ 10⁴, correlate rank with U(p)/log²p.

title: R-zeros have small h(−4p): 13 of 14 below the median (nominal binomial tail ≈ 0.0009)
why: Confirms the χ_{−4p} fit's prediction: (★)-hard primes have small class number of Q(√−p); the extreme version (Siegel-zero-like L(1,χ_{−4p})) would be the hardest (★) instances — ties the campaign's Siegel-dichotomy memo to data.
first_step: Extend to R-zeros beyond 10¹⁰ if the census is extended; compute the joint (h(−4p), L(1,χ_p)) quantile and see whether R-zeros are extreme in the joint distribution.

title: Elsholtz–Tao normalisation: average U(p) grows like log³p, not log²p
connection: ET (arXiv:1107.1010, verified abstract) prove N log²N ≪ Σ_{p≤N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N (f ordered), i.e. average f(p) ≍ log³p up to log log; our median U(p)/log²p rises 1.33 (p≈10⁶) → 1.54 (p≈10⁷), ratio ≈ log-ratio 1.17, consistent with log³.
why: All hardness rankings across different sizes should use U(p)/log³p (or the fitted Euler-product model); the log² normalisation in several items here is only valid within a narrow range.
first_step: Refit min/median of U(p)/log³p and U(p)/(log³p·loglog p) over dyadic ranges 10³…10⁸ to see which normalisation is flat.

title: Sign flip between p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 3 (mod 4): QR-ness of small primes helps at 3 (mod 4), hurts at 1 (mod 4)
connection: β_q are uniformly positive for p ≡ 3 (4) and mostly negative for p ≡ 1 (4) (for U, k₁, k₂, Uv).
why: At p ≡ 3 (4), (q/p) = χ_{−p}(q) (imaginary field Q(√−p)) and enters positively: U grows with L(1,χ_{−p}) ∝ h(−p)/√p; at p ≡ 1 (4), (q/p) = χ_p(q) (real field Q(√p)) and enters negatively: U shrinks as L(1,χ_p) = 2h(p)log ε_p/√p grows. Imaginary-quadratic L-values help, real-quadratic ones hurt.
first_step: Fit a model U ∝ L(1,χ_{−p})^{a} at p ≡ 3 and L(1,χ_p)^{b} at p ≡ 1 and compare |a|, |b| (≈ 0.4 vs ≈ 0.3?).

title: The χ_p correlation persists out of sample at 10⁶ and 10⁷
connection: Spearman(U(p), log L₃₁(1,χ_p)) = −0.62 (156 primes ≡ 1 (4) in [10⁶, 10⁶+4000]) and −0.69 (113 primes in [10⁷, 10⁷+4000]); k₁ −0.66/−0.75, k₂ −0.38/−0.36 — same strength as at ≤ 2·10⁵ (rank correlations; the fitted exponent α ≈ −0.30 itself was not re-estimated).
why: The correlation is scale-stable, so the χ_p dependence is not small-number noise; whether the exponent is stable needs the refit in the first step.
first_step: Push to 10⁹ windows (count program ≈ 100 s per prime there) and track whether the exponent α ≈ −0.3 drifts.

title: The (★) mean constant vs BM mean: R/M_BM ≈ 1.31 (p ≤ 12 000) and 1.22 (20 000–30 000)
connection: Mean ratio of R(p) to the BM main term drifts down with p (M₀ ratio 1.26 → 1.18).
why: If R/M_BM → 1 the BM term is asymptotically the right mean (FRONTIER: M_BM ∼ M₀ under GRH); the drift rate measures the secondary term.
first_step: Compute R/M_BM at windows 10⁵, 10⁶, 3·10⁶ (script scales linearly per prime).

title: Erdős–Graham style: least common denominator of ES solutions vs smooth numbers
connection: minlcm(p)/p (least common denominator over solutions, divided by p) — is it always smooth (all prime factors ≤ p^{1/2})? Practical?
why: Egyptian-fraction denominators tend to be smooth; a smoothness law for minlcm would give a search space ('only smooth L need be tried') for certificates.
first_step: Factor minlcm(p)/p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ and record the max of log P⁺/log p.

title: Cohen–Lenstra heuristic for h(p) irrelevant; regulator heuristics (Hooley) relevant
connection: Since ES counts follow L(1,χ_p) and h(p) is mostly 1, the distribution of ES counts at p ≡ 1 (4) inherits the distribution of log ε_p/√p (Hooley's conjecture on the average of real quadratic class numbers × regulators).
why: Gives a 'distribution of hardness' prediction: P(U(p) small) ≈ P(L(1,χ_p) large) which is doubly-exponentially small in the size (Granville–Soundararajan distribution of L(1,χ)).
first_step: Compare the empirical tail of residual log U with the Granville–Soundararajan tail for log L(1,χ_p) scaled by α ≈ 0.3.
